prize_parts.citation: for the development of halide perovskites as solution-processed semiconductor absorbers for efficient solar cells

statement.case_for: After the full first round I keep B016 with Miyasaka, Park and Snaith. It is still the only configuration with more than one explicit supporter, and more importantly the attribution has held up under scrutiny: Aqvist, Brzezinski and Zou, who differ with me on ranking, independently name the same trio, which almost never happens in a crowded field. The discovery is a new semiconductor family that is both scientifically explicable (corner-sharing ABX3 structure, strong absorption, long diffusion lengths, defect tolerance, tunable gap) and generative: efficiency rose from a few percent in 2009 to above 25 percent, and the same material now underlies LEDs, detectors and tandem cells. That is the kind of previously unforeseen opportunity a Nobel citation should point to. The chain of credit is also traceable: Miyasaka's first perovskite-sensitized cell, Park's 2012 solid-state step, and Snaith's mesosuperstructured and planar architectures showing that the absorber, not the dye-cell scaffold, does the work. I have tried to test my own preference against the objections raised in round 1 and I judge that the objections concern the deployment of the technology, not the discovery.
statement.case_against: The objections from Aili, Aqvist, Brzezinski, Chabes and Somfai deserve weight. Operational stability and lead content are unresolved, no module has yet shown a silicon-like lifetime, and a committee could reasonably say that recognition in 2026 is early. Gratzel, Seok and Kanatzidis all have credible claims and any trio will look somewhat arbitrary to them. Much of the progress is device engineering, which could be read as physics or materials science. I also recognise that I am a physicist favouring a device-and-limit argument, and the chair should not let that tilt the group. Finally, B016 still has only two explicit supporters, so I cannot claim a path to five votes without movement from the members who currently hold B045, B029 and B043.

responses.point: Aqvist is uncomfortable with maturity (stability, lead, deployment) and says Gratzel, Seok and Kanatzidis make the Miyasaka-Snaith-Park chain less clean than it looks.
responses.response: I accept the second point in part: Gratzel's dye-cell lineage and Kanatzidis's lead-halide structural work are real, and I would ask the group to word the citation around the perovskite absorber so it does not depend on the dye-cell history. I do not accept the first as a bar. The prize question is the discovery and its demonstrated scientific consequences, and a decade of worldwide replication and spin-off devices is such a record. On B029, I keep my round-1 question: the Born-Oppenheimer scheme now does much of the daily work, and your own case concedes that the argument rests on the conceptual step. If the committee wants a second part, I would sooner see it on a clinically proven topic than a third computational award since 1998.

responses.point: Sparr separates the established in vitro thermodynamics of condensates (multivalency, saturation concentration, coexistence) from the contested in vivo cases, and treats a young field as normal.
responses.response: That separation is the strongest form of your case and I take it seriously: the in vitro framework is chemistry in the full sense, and I would drop the objection that it belongs to cell biology. My remaining difficulty is the citation. Hyman, Brangwynne and Rosen leave out Pappu and Mittag, who supplied the sequence-to-behaviour physical chemistry, and a citation limited to the in vitro principle would not describe the work that made the field prominent. I hold B069 as my first alternative, not my preference, because the interpretation of what is actually phase separated in cells remains a larger open question than anything perovskites face, where the dispute is about lifetime and not about what the material is.

responses.point: Aili prefers B045 (Cullis and Langer) on demonstrated clinical impact, and notes the 2023 Medicine prize recognised nucleoside modification, not the vehicle.
responses.response: I agree that B045 has the strongest demonstrated consequences of any shortlisted entry and that the Medicine prize does not cover the vehicle. That is why it is my other alternative. The obstacle is the cut: Sparr's trio (Cullis, Hope, Madden) and your pair (Cullis, Langer) disagree on who is decisive, and Cullis is the only name both share. If the committee can establish that ionizable lipids with rapid-mixing formulation are the decisive step, I could support B045 with Cullis, Hope and Madden, but I cannot yet defend leaving out Langer and Anderson, whose lipidoid work enabled the first siRNA products, without that evidence.

responses.point: Zou moved from mesoporous silica to B016 and argues the prize concerns the discovery and not whether a module is on the market.
responses.response: I agree and note it is the key principle on maturity: the group did not wait for commercial lithium-ion maturity either. I would add to your structural-chemistry argument that the central claim is checked by diffraction and electronic-structure calculations, so the mechanism is not merely empirical. Your own case-against list on ion migration and phase segregation is a fair statement of what remains open, and I would want the citation wording to avoid implying that the long-term device problem is solved.

responses.point: Somfai prefers B052 (Buchwald and Hartwig), arguing it is clean and mature, and doubts B016 because six names are credible.
responses.response: The C-N coupling case is the cleanest on maturity and attribution and I concede both. My difficulty is the one you name yourself, which Brzezinski shares: the 2010 prize rewarded the Pd-catalysed cross-coupling idea, so the committee would need to argue that the amido-palladium problem and the ligand logic are a distinct achievement. That is a matter of judgement, but it is a higher burden than the one B016 carries. On B016 the six-name concern is real, yet the same trio appears in four independent openings, which tells me the committee, not only the supporters, can identify who did the decisive early steps.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will treat stability and lead toxicity as a reason to wait, or accept the discovery and a decade of replication as sufficient.
Whether Gratzel, Seok or Kanatzidis should displace Snaith or Park, and whether the trio holds if expert reports on priority between 2009 and 2012 point elsewhere.
Whether a path to five votes exists for any single configuration, given eight distinct positions in round 1, and whether a two-part pairing is realistic under the three-person cap.
Whether the in vivo picture for B069 and the clinical record for B043 will mature enough to matter in this year's ballot.
statement.conflict_note: Unchanged from round 1. As chair I have no tie to any credited person or to the perovskite groups. My work on quantum-dot thermoelectrics and nanowires at Lund is adjacent to semiconductor photophysics, and my physics bias toward device and limit-based arguments could favour B016. I share Lund with Somfai and Sparr, which I do not treat as a recusal issue for these candidates. I seek no recusal.
